list.title: Morning at the Market
list.summary: Sari helps her father shop for a week of food.
list.passage:
Sari and her father left the house before the sun was fully up. The air was cool, and the street was still quiet. They walked to the traditional market because Saturday was the day they bought food for the whole week. Sari carried a cloth bag on her shoulder. Her father carried a bigger bag and a list written on a small piece of paper.

The market was already busy when they arrived. Sellers called out prices in loud, friendly voices. The smell of fried tempeh mixed with the smell of fresh herbs. Sari stayed close to her father so she would not get lost between the stalls. First they stopped at the vegetable stall. A woman in a green apron smiled at them and held up a bunch of leaves.

"The spinach is very fresh today," she said. "It came from the hills this morning."

Sari's father asked the price and chose a large bunch. He also bought carrots, tomatoes, and a small cabbage. Sari helped put the vegetables into the bag. The cabbage was heavier than she expected, and she laughed when the bag swung against her leg. Her father laughed too and took the heavy side of the bag so she could walk more easily.

Next they visited the fruit stall. Mangoes were piled like a yellow hill. Sari pointed at the small sweet ones she liked best. Her father bought four and let her choose them herself. She pressed each mango gently with her thumb. The seller nodded and said, "Good choice. Those will be soft and sweet by tomorrow."

At the fish stall, crushed ice shone under the bright lights. Sari did not like the strong smell, but she watched carefully while her father picked two fish. He checked the eyes and the gills, the way his own father had taught him years ago. "Fresh fish should look clear, not cloudy," he told Sari. She repeated the sentence quietly so she would remember it next time.

Before they left the market, they bought eggs, rice, and a bunch of green onions. Sari read the last line of the list out loud so nothing would be forgotten. A motorbike moved slowly through the narrow path, and they stepped aside to let it pass. An old man who sold brooms waved at Sari. She lifted her free hand and waved back.

On the way home they stopped for warm soy milk. Sari held the cup with both hands while her father paid. People passed with baskets, boxes, and small children. She felt proud that she had helped with the shopping. The list was finished, the bags were full, and breakfast was waiting at home. The market had been loud and crowded, but walking beside her father made the whole morning feel calm.

list.title: The Rainy Bus Ride
list.summary: Dimas rides across the city to visit his grandmother.
list.passage:
Dimas stood under the bus stop roof and watched the rain hit the road. He was going to his grandmother's house on the other side of the city. His backpack held a book, a bottle of water, and a box of cookies his mother had wrapped in paper. The cookies were for his grandmother, and he had promised not to open the box on the way.

The bus arrived ten minutes late. Water ran down its windows, and the door opened with a tired sound. Dimas climbed the steps, paid the driver, and looked for an empty seat. Most seats were full. A woman with a sleeping child sat near the front. Two students shared earphones in the middle. Dimas found a seat by the window, next to an older man who was reading a newspaper.

"Wet day," the man said.

"Yes," Dimas answered. "I hope the rain slows down before I have to walk."

The bus moved through deep puddles. Cars waited at every light. Dimas wiped a small circle on the glass so he could see the shops outside. He saw a bakery, a phone shop, and a school with a blue gate. At the school, children in raincoats ran toward a covered walkway. One of them slipped, then stood up and laughed. Dimas smiled. He remembered doing the same thing when he was younger.

Halfway through the ride, the bus stopped for a long time. The driver announced that a tree branch had fallen across the next street. People groaned, but nobody shouted. The man beside Dimas folded his newspaper. "We can wait," he said. "Being angry will not move the branch."

Dimas opened his book, but he did not read many pages. He kept thinking about his grandmother's kitchen. She would make fried bananas and ask about school. She would want to hear every small story, not only the big ones. He touched the cookie box in his bag to make sure it was still closed.

After twenty minutes, workers pulled the branch aside and the bus rolled forward again. The rain was lighter now. When Dimas got off at his stop, the sky was pale grey instead of dark. He opened his umbrella, walked two blocks, and saw his grandmother already standing in the doorway. She waved with both hands. Dimas waved back and walked faster. The ride had been slow, but the warm light in her house made the waiting feel worth it.

list.title: Saturday at the Corner Shop
list.summary: Rafi helps Bu Sinta in the shop and learns to give clear answers.
list.passage:
Rafi stopped at the corner shop every weekday morning on his way to school. The bell over the door rang, and the owner, Bu Sinta, always looked up from her notebook. The shop was small. Shelves of soap, noodles, and bottled tea reached almost to the ceiling. A fan turned in the corner and moved the warm air from one side of the room to the other.

"The usual?" Bu Sinta asked.

"Yes, please," Rafi said. He bought a carton of milk for his little sister and a piece of bread for himself. His mother had started a new shift at the clinic, so breakfast at home was shorter now. The shop had become part of the morning.

While Bu Sinta counted the change, Rafi looked at the handwritten prices taped to the shelf. Eggs had gone up. Sugar had stayed the same. He did not need either one today, but he liked knowing. Bu Sinta noticed.

"You read those labels more carefully than some adults," she said. "If you ever want to help me on Saturday, I will pay you in bread and a lesson."

Rafi smiled. "What kind of lesson?"

"How not to lose count when three customers talk at once."

That Saturday he came back after he finished his homework. Bu Sinta gave him an apron that was too long. He folded the waistband twice. His first job was to stack the bottled water in straight rows. Then a customer asked for detergent, and Rafi found it on the bottom shelf. He said the price clearly and waited while the man checked his coins.

At noon the shop grew busy. A girl wanted candy. A neighbor wanted rice. Someone asked for a brand of tea that was finished. Bu Sinta did not look worried. "Tell them what we do have," she said. "A clear answer is better than a long search."

Rafi repeated that to himself. When he did not know a price, he asked instead of guessing. When he gave the wrong change once, he noticed before the customer left, apologized, and fixed it. Bu Sinta nodded. "Mistakes are part of the work. Hiding them is the real problem."

By the afternoon his feet hurt and his apron was dusty. Bu Sinta handed him a warm roll and the coins they had agreed on. Rafi put the coins in his pocket and ate the roll on the step outside. The bell rang again as another customer entered. He already knew he would come back next Saturday. The shop was loud and narrow, but every task had a clear end, and he liked being useful.

list.title: Washing Day on the Balcony
list.summary: Dina helps her mother wash, hang, and fold the clothes.
list.passage:
On Sunday the sun came out after three wet days, and Dina's mother said it was time to wash everything. Sheets, school shirts, towels, and two pillowcases waited in a basket by the bathroom door. Their apartment did not have a yard. The washing machine stood in a corner of the kitchen, and the drying line was on the balcony.

Dina carried the basket while her mother measured the soap. "Too much soap does not make clothes cleaner," her mother said. "It only makes them hard to rinse." Dina watched the cup. She wanted to pour more, because the bottle smelled nice, but she stopped at the line her mother had shown her.

The machine hummed. While they waited, they wiped the table and swept the floor. Dina's little brother, Yoga, tried to help and mostly moved dust from one place to another. Their mother did not scold him. She gave him a small cloth and a low shelf he could actually reach.

When the machine stopped, the clothes were heavy with water. Dina and her mother lifted them into a basin and carried the basin to the balcony. The line was already full of pegs. Dina shook each shirt before she hung it, so the cloth would not dry in a twisted shape. Yoga handed her pegs, two at a time, and announced the colors as if they were a game.

A wind moved through the balcony and lifted the edge of a sheet. The sheet brushed Dina's face and made her laugh. From the next balcony, a neighbor waved over a pot of chili plants. Below them, the street was bright. Someone was repairing a bicycle. Someone else was selling iced drinks from a cart.

"Do not lean on the railing," her mother said, not sharply, just as a habit. Dina stepped back and clipped the last towel. Her arms ached in a pleasant way. The line of clothes looked like flags.

In the late afternoon they brought the dry clothes inside. The shirts smelled like sunlight. Dina folded the sleeves the way her mother had taught her, edge to edge. One sock was missing. They found it behind the basin, still damp, and hung it alone on a chair near the window.

"Washing is never finished in one move," her mother said. "You wash, you hang, you fold, and then you notice the one thing you missed."

Dina put the folded shirts in the cupboard. Tomorrow morning her uniform would be ready, and she would know exactly whose hands had made it ready. That felt better than grabbing it from a pile.

list.title: The Long Way Home
list.summary: Intan walks home along the canal and finds a loose bridge board.
list.passage:
Usually Intan took the main road home from school. It was straight, noisy, and fast. On Thursday her friend Yusuf had football practice, so she walked alone and decided to try the long way. The long way followed a canal, then a row of houses with plants in tin cans, then a small bridge.

The canal water was low and slow. Dragonflies hovered over it. Intan kept her bag on both shoulders and did not walk too close to the edge. A woman was rinsing a bucket. She nodded at Intan, and Intan nodded back. Nobody else seemed in a hurry.

At the houses, an old man sat on a stool fixing a radio. The radio crackled, then found a song, then lost it again. He looked up. "If you are going to the bridge, the middle board is loose," he said. "Step on the side."

"Thank you," Intan said. She was glad he had told her. She had almost walked across without looking.

She tested the bridge with one foot. The middle board dipped. She stepped to the right, where the nails looked newer, and crossed. On the other side a cat watched her from a wall and did not move. Intan liked that the cat was not afraid, only uninterested.

The long way added ten minutes. She did not mind. On the main road, motorbikes passed so close that she had to think about traffic the whole time. Here she could think about the science worksheet in her bag. She tried to remember the difference between a solid and a liquid. The canal helped. The water had a shape only because the banks held it. Take away the banks, and it would spread. She smiled at her own example. Maybe she would write it down before she forgot.

Near her street she bought a small bunch of bananas from a cart. The seller knew her mother and added one extra banana without comment. Intan said thank you twice.

At home her mother was surprised. "You are late. Was the road crowded?"

"I took the long way," Intan said. "A man told me about a loose board, and I saw a cat who did not care about me at all."

Her mother laughed and took the bananas. "The long way is fine if you tell me first next time. I like knowing which road has you."

Intan agreed. She set her bag down, washed her hands, and wrote the canal example at the top of her worksheet before dinner could wash it out of her mind.

options: Her mother asked her to buy bananas.

options: The middle board of the bridge was loose.

options: Intan to stay on the main road forever

list.title: Partners for the Project
list.summary: Raka and Nia make a poster and present it together.
list.passage:
On Monday morning, Ms. Lestari wrote a new task on the board. The class would make a poster about a helpful habit. Students had to work in pairs, finish the poster by Friday, and explain it in front of the class. A few students cheered. A few students sank lower in their chairs. Raka belonged to the second group. He liked drawing, but he did not like speaking to a crowd.

His partner was Nia, a girl who always had her notes in order. She sat down beside him and opened a clean page. "We should pick one habit and stay with it," she said. "If we choose too many ideas, the poster will look messy."

Raka thought for a moment. "What about drinking water?" he asked. "People forget it when they are busy."

Nia nodded. "That is simple and useful. You can draw the pictures. I can write the short sentences. Then we can practice the talk together."

They met in the library after school on Tuesday and Wednesday. Raka sketched a bottle, a clock, and a student at a desk. At first the bottle looked like a strange vase. Nia did not laugh in a mean way. She pointed at the neck of the bottle and said, "Make this part narrower." Raka tried again, and the second drawing was better. He added blue drops and a small smile on the student's face.

Nia wrote five sentences. Each one was short enough to read from the back of the room. She also made a list of words they might need if a classmate asked a question. Raka read the list out loud until the words felt easy in his mouth. They practiced once in the library and once in an empty classroom, where their voices sounded bigger.

On Friday their hands shook a little, but they stood up together. Raka held the poster. Nia spoke first, then Raka explained the pictures. When he forgot one line, he looked at the bottle he had drawn and remembered. The class clapped. Ms. Lestari said their message was clear and their teamwork was easy to see.

After class, Raka rolled the poster carefully. "I still get nervous," he told Nia.

"Me too," she said. "Nervous and ready can happen at the same time."

list.title: Quiet Afternoon in the Library
list.summary: Amira looks for a new book and helps another reader.
list.passage:
The school library was the coolest room on a hot Thursday. Fans turned slowly above the shelves, and the floor smelled a little like old paper and floor cleaner. Amira had come to return a storybook and to find something new. She liked the library because nobody asked her to hurry.

Mrs. Dewi, the librarian, scanned the returned book and smiled. "You finished this one quickly. Are you looking for another adventure, or do you want something true this time?"

Amira was not sure. She walked past the shelves with her finger hovering near the spines. Some titles were funny. Some were about space. One thick book showed a volcano on the cover, and she pulled it out. The first page had too many hard words, so she put it back. She did not feel bad about that. Mrs. Dewi always said that choosing a book was part of reading.

Near the window she found a thinner book about a girl who built a small garden in cans and buckets. The pictures were bright, and the sentences were clear. Amira sat at a table and read the first chapter. The girl in the book lived in a city apartment. She had no yard, but she still grew tomatoes. Amira thought of the narrow balcony at her own home. Maybe a tomato plant could live there too.

A boy at the next table was sounding out a word under his breath. He stopped, frowned, and tried again. Amira knew that feeling. She slid a scrap of paper toward him and wrote the word in two parts. He whispered thank you and kept going. Mrs. Dewi noticed, but she only gave them a small nod. In the library, help was supposed to be quiet.

Amira read until the bell for the last class. She marked her page with the library card and brought the book to the desk. "I will take this one," she said.

"Bring it back when the tomatoes in the story are ready to eat," Mrs. Dewi said.

Amira laughed. She was not sure she understood the joke completely, but she liked it. She put the book in her bag and stepped into the bright hallway. The library stayed behind her, cool and quiet, like a room that would wait until she returned.

list.title: Shoes for the Match
list.summary: Andi and his sister find a missing sports shoe before practice.
list.passage:
The class match was on Friday, and Andi could not find his sports shoes. He searched under the bed, behind the door, and inside a box of old toys. He found one shoe. The other was gone. Practice started at four. Without both shoes, the coach would tell him to sit out.

His father was still at work. His older sister, Wulan, was at the kitchen table with her own books. Andi stood in the doorway in his school socks and tried not to sound panicked.

"I only have one," he said.

Wulan closed her book. "When did you last wear them?"

"Tuesday. We ran laps. I think I put them on the porch to dry."

They went to the porch. The mat was empty. A neighbor's dog sometimes carried things, but the dog was asleep and looked too innocent to question. Wulan checked the shoe rack again, then the bathroom, then the bag Andi had used on Tuesday. The missing shoe was not in the bag. A damp sock was.

"Think smaller," Wulan said. "Where would one shoe hide if it fell?"

Andi got on his knees and looked under the porch step. Something white was stuck between a brick and the wall. He pulled. It was the shoe, dusty and a little chewed at the lace, but still a shoe. He held it up as if he had won a prize.

"The dog," he said.

"Maybe," Wulan said. "Or you kicked it there and forgot. Either way, it needs a wash."

They cleaned it with a wet cloth and soap. Andi worked on the dust. Wulan picked the dirt out of the tread with a stick. The lace could not be saved, so Wulan took a spare lace from her own old pair and showed Andi how to pull it through the holes without skipping one. He watched once, then did the rest himself.

It was three forty when they finished. Andi put both shoes on and jumped twice to test them. They felt even. He grabbed his water bottle.

"Thank you," he said at the door.

"Score one goal and we are even," Wulan said.

Andi did not score. He did pass the ball twice to a teammate who did. After the match he told Wulan the truth. She shrugged. "Then the shoes did their job. They got you on the field."

list.title: The Plant Experiment
list.summary: Lala's group tests what bean plants need to grow.
list.passage:
Ms. Putri wanted the class to see what plants actually need. She gave each group three small pots, soil, and bean seeds. "Same seeds, same soil, different treatment," she said. "Write what you do. Do not trust your memory."

Lala's group included Bima and Sinta. They labeled the pots A, B, and C with tape. Pot A would get water and sunlight. Pot B would get water but stay in a cupboard. Pot C would get sunlight but no water. Sinta wrote the plan in a notebook. Bima wanted to water all of them "just a little," because he felt sorry for pot C. Lala shook her head.

"If we change the plan, we will not learn anything," she said. "Pot C is supposed to be dry. We can plant more beans at home if you want."

They set the pots on Monday. Every day at the end of school, Sinta checked them and wrote one sentence. On Wednesday, pot A showed a pale hook pushing out of the soil. Pot B showed a thinner hook, almost white. Pot C showed nothing. Bima looked disappointed and proud at the same time. The plan was working, even the sad part.

By Friday, pot A was green and standing up. Pot B had grown taller but looked weak, and its leaves were yellow. "It is searching for light," Ms. Putri said. "It spent its energy on height because the seed only has a little food inside." Pot C was still only soil. Sinta drew all three pots and labeled the differences without using the word "bad." Ms. Putri had asked them to describe, not judge.

On Monday they moved pot B into the light and gave pot C a careful drink. "Now you are not starting a new experiment," Ms. Putri said. "You are asking a second question. Can they recover?" Two of the students guessed no. Lala guessed yes for pot B and no for pot C.

She was half right. Pot B turned greener in four days. Pot C never sprouted. The seed had dried out. The group wrote that water and light do different jobs, and that a seed cannot wait forever. Bima still felt a little sorry. He also said he would not forget to water the herbs on his aunt's balcony. The experiment had been about beans. It ended up being about attention.

list.title: Lunch Under the Tree
list.summary: Nadia and her friends share lunch when one of them forgets hers.
list.passage:
The cafeteria was full, and the line reached the door, so Nadia and her friends carried their lunch boxes to the tree behind the classroom. The ground was dry. Roots made the sitting uneven, but the shade was better than the noisy hall. They had twenty minutes before the bell.

Nadia opened her box and found rice, egg, and cucumber. Her friend Omar had fried noodles. Their classmate Tia had forgotten her box at home and was trying to pretend she was not hungry. She drank water and said she would wait until later.

Omar pushed his box toward the middle without making a speech. "I cannot finish this," he said, which was not true. He always finished it. Tia looked at him, then at Nadia. Nadia tore her cucumber into three pieces and added one piece to the noodles. "Then we share," she said. "Otherwise you will have too much, and that is wasteful."

Tia laughed, because the excuse was thin and kind. She ate slowly, as if she wanted the sharing to stay small. Nobody asked why the box had been left at home. Nadia was glad. Some reasons were not for the lunch break.

While they ate, they watched a group of younger students play a guessing game near the fence. One boy kept shouting the answer too early, and his friends groaned. Tia said, "He is not wrong. He is just fast in the wrong place." The sentence made them all quiet for a second, then Omar repeated it and pointed at himself. He had done the same thing in math that morning.

The bell rang earlier than they wanted. They packed the boxes, brushed crumbs off their skirts and trousers, and checked the ground so ants would not have a feast. Tia held the empty noodle box to return it. "I will bring extra fruit tomorrow," she said.

"You do not have to pay us back," Nadia said.

"I know," Tia said. "I want to. Sharing works better when it can move in more than one direction."

They walked back into the bright corridor. The cafeteria line was finally short. Nadia did not regret missing it. Lunch under the tree had been uneven ground, a small cucumber, and a friend who was no longer pretending. That was enough for one noon.

list.title: A Morning in the Rainforest
list.summary: Farah visits the forest and learns to wait quietly.
list.passage:
The ranger asked the visitors to keep their voices low. They were standing on a wooden walkway above the wet forest floor, and the morning mist still hung between the trees. Farah pulled her jacket closer. She had joined a student trip to see the rainforest, and she wanted to remember every sound.

"Look, but do not touch," the ranger said. "Some plants protect themselves with sharp hairs or strong smells. The forest is not a garden that we arrange. It is a home that was here before we arrived."

Farah wrote that sentence in her notebook. Below the walkway, brown leaves covered the ground. A beetle with a shiny green back crossed a root and disappeared. Somewhere above them, a bird called twice, then stopped, as if it was listening too.

The ranger pointed to a tall tree with wide roots that looked like walls. "Those roots hold the tree up in thin soil," he explained. "Rain here is heavy. Without strong roots, the tree would fall." He also showed them a vine that climbed toward the light. Plants on the forest floor do not always get enough sun, so some of them grow upward and borrow the height of others.

Farah had expected monkeys to swing past at once. They did not. For a long time the group saw only leaves, insects, and one small frog no bigger than a coin. A boy behind her sighed. The ranger heard it and smiled. "Wild animals do not perform for us. If we are patient and quiet, they may come close. If we are loud, they will stay hidden, and they are right to do so."

They waited. Water dripped from a leaf onto Farah's sleeve. Then a branch moved, and a dark shape sat high in a tree. It was an orangutan, resting with one arm over a bent knee. Nobody spoke. The orangutan looked down for a moment, calm and unhurried, and then turned its face away. Farah's heart beat fast, but she kept her mouth closed.

On the bus back to school she opened her notebook and added one more line. The most exciting part of the forest was not a show. It was the feeling of being a guest. She wanted to tell her class that patience had given them one clear look, and that one look was enough.

list.title: Evening in the Rice Fields
list.summary: Bima walks the fields with his grandfather after school.
list.passage:
When the sun dropped lower, the rice fields turned gold. Pak Rahman walked along the narrow path between the water and the young plants. His grandson, Bima, followed with a stick in one hand. They were not hunting anything. The stick was only for balance when the mud was slippery.

"Rice looks simple from the road," Pak Rahman said. "Up close, it is a long promise. We plant, we wait, we watch the water, and we hope the rain comes at the right time."

Bima looked at the green rows. They seemed endless. He knew his grandfather woke up early during planting season. He had not known how many small jobs filled the hours. Today they checked for insects, pulled a few weeds, and made sure the water was not too deep. A bird stood in the shallow water and tilted its head. Pak Rahman did not chase it away. "That one eats pests," he said. "Not every visitor is a problem."

They sat on a dry bank and shared sweet tea from a bottle. The air smelled like wet soil and cut grass. In the distance, someone rode a motorbike along the village road, and the sound faded. Bima asked why his grandfather still farmed when the work was so hard.

Pak Rahman was quiet for a while. Then he patted the ground beside him. "This field fed my parents. It fed me. If I take care of it, it can feed you too, or it can teach you where food begins. Both things matter. A person can choose another job later. A person should not forget the ground."

Bima did not answer at once. He watched a dragonfly land on a rice leaf and lift off again. School would start again on Monday, and he had homework waiting at home. Still, he was glad he had come. The field was not only a picture for a holiday. It was his family's work, repeated season after season.

On the walk back, Bima carried the empty bottle and matched his grandfather's slow steps. The sky was pink at the edges. Frogs began to call from the ditches. Tomorrow the plants would still need water, and the weeds would try again. For tonight, the gold light on the field was enough of a reward.

list.title: Stones at Low Tide
list.summary: Alya walks the uncovered beach and learns to leave the animals alone.
list.passage:
The sea had pulled back so far that the beach looked wider than usual. Dark rocks that were normally underwater sat in the sun, covered with shells and slippery green weed. Pak Joko, who lived near the shore, had agreed to walk with the youth club for one hour. "Low tide is a door," he said. "It opens, and then it closes. We do not stay for the closing."

Alya stepped carefully. Her sandals were in her hand because they slid on the weed. In a shallow pool she saw a crab no bigger than a coin. It lifted its claws and sidestepped under a stone. She wanted to move the stone. Pak Joko shook his head.

"If you lift the roof off a house, you should be ready to be the weather," he said. "Leave it. Look from the side."

Alya crouched and waited. The crab came out again, decided she was not a threat, and began picking at something too small to name. Farther along, the group found sea snails stuck hard to the rock. A boy tried to pull one. It did not move. Pak Joko told him that the snail's grip was its way of staying alive until the water returned. "Strength is not always running," he said. "Sometimes it is holding on."

They saw a starfish in a pool near the edge of the wet sand. Its color was dull until the water moved over it. Then the color deepened. Alya wrote that in her notebook: some things look plain until the sea touches them. She also wrote the time. Pak Joko had asked every student to notice when they arrived and when they left.

The wind changed. A thin line of foam began to crawl back toward the rocks. It was not dramatic. It was steady. Pak Joko clapped once. "The door is closing. Up to the dry sand."

They walked back above the tide line and sat on a low wall. Alya's feet were sandy and cold. She was glad they had not chased the crab or forced the snail. The beach would be ordinary again by evening, the rocks hidden, the pools gone. What she kept was the hour when the sea had trusted them with its floor, and they had tried to deserve it.

options: The crab was using it as a home.

options: Stay alive until the water returned

options: A line of foam moved back toward the rocks.

list.title: The Path Up the Hill
list.summary: Gilang and Rara climb the hill behind the village.
list.passage:
Behind the village, a hill rose in a slow curve. From the bottom it looked easy. Gilang and his cousin Rara started climbing after breakfast, with a bottle of water and two boiled eggs wrapped in paper. Their uncle had said the view was worth the path, and that the path was worth more than the view.

The first part went through tall grass. Insects jumped ahead of their feet. Rara talked the whole way, about school, about a film, about the dog that had followed them and then given up. Gilang answered when he had breath. He had not expected to lose his breath so soon.

Halfway up, the grass became shrubs and the path turned into packed dirt with stones. They stopped at a flat rock. The eggs were still warm. They ate them and shared the water without finishing it. "Leave some for the top," Rara said. "The top is where people get careless."

A goat stood on the slope above them, chewing, watching with yellow eyes. It did not come closer. Gilang was relieved and a little insulted. He had wanted a story about a wild animal. A goat that ignored them was still a true story. He decided it counted.

Near the top the wind was stronger and the trees were shorter. The village appeared below in pieces: the tin roofs, the school field, the road that led to the market. Their own house was a brown rectangle beside a mango tree. Rara pointed. "We hang the washing there. From here it is only a white dot."

Gilang sat down because his legs had started to shake. The shaking was not fear. It was effort leaving the muscles. He drank the rest of his share of water and felt it go all the way down. The view was wide, but what he noticed most was the quiet. No motorbikes. No one calling his name from a doorway.

On the way down they went slower than on the way up. Loose stones slid under their sandals. Rara stopped talking as much. At the bottom, their uncle was repairing a fence. He looked at their dusty knees and nodded. "You made it."

"The goat did not care," Gilang said.

"Good," their uncle said. "The hill is not a performance. You climbed it. That is the whole point."

questions.question: Why did Rara say they should save some water?
options: People get careless at the top.
The bottle leaked in the grass.
Their uncle wanted it back full.

questions.question: What did the goat do?
options: It followed them to the top.

questions.question: What did their uncle say was the point of the climb?
options: They had seen a wild animal.
They had found the white dot of washing.
They had raced each other down.

list.title: A Sudden Rain at the Lake
list.summary: Hana and her uncle watch the lake until the weather changes.
list.passage:
The lake was a twenty-minute walk from the guesthouse. Hana and her uncle had planned to sit on the wooden platform and watch the fishermen. The sky was pale when they left. A few clouds sat on the hills, but they did not look serious.

They rented two cups of hot ginger drink from a stall and carried them carefully. The platform was old. Some boards had been replaced, and those boards were lighter than the others. Hana sat on a darker one and let her feet hang above the water. Small fish gathered under the shade of the platform, waiting for crumbs that nobody offered.

A fisherman in a narrow boat threw a net with a motion that looked easy and was not. The net opened like a flower and sank. He pulled it back almost empty, shrugged, and tried again. Hana's uncle said the man was not failing. He was reading the lake. "Empty is information," he said. "It tells him where not to stay."

The wind arrived before the rain. It pushed the ginger steam sideways and made the boat knock softly against its rope. Then the hills disappeared. Rain came across the water in a silver sheet. People on the platform laughed and ran for the stall's roof. Hana and her uncle ran too, holding the cups out so they would not spill on their clothes.

Under the roof, the rain was loud on the tin. The fisherman did not come in at once. He covered his basket, turned the boat, and rowed to shore with his shoulders bent. When he finally stepped under the roof, he shook his head and smiled at no one in particular. "The lake changed its mind," he said.

They waited. Hana finished the ginger drink, which was no longer hot. Her uncle bought a small bag of fried bananas to share with the people crowded beside them. A child stared at the bag until her uncle offered one. The child's mother nodded her thanks.

When the rain thinned, the hills returned, darker than before. The platform shone. Hana walked back onto it and saw the fish still there, as if nothing important had happened. She wrote one line in her phone notes before the screen got wet: the weather can change the plan and leave the place itself untouched.

questions.question: What did Hana's uncle say an empty net tells a fisherman?
options: The lake is closed for the day.
That the ginger drink is ready
That the rain has already passed

questions.question: Where did people go when the rain arrived?
options: Back to the guesthouse at once

list.title: The Kite on the Roof
list.summary: Lina's kite gets stuck, and she asks for help.
list.passage:
Lina had built the kite herself from thin paper, two sticks, and a long tail made of ribbon. She had drawn a red sun in the middle. On Sunday afternoon the wind was finally strong enough, so she and her cousin Ari took the kite to the open field behind their houses.

The first try failed. The kite jumped, twisted, and fell into the grass. Ari laughed, then stopped when he saw Lina's face. "The tail is too short," he said. "It cannot balance." They tied on another ribbon. The second try was better. The kite rose above the fence, above the banana trees, and tugged at the string in Lina's hands. She shouted without meaning to. For ten bright minutes everything worked.

Then the wind changed. A harder gust pulled the kite toward the row of houses. Lina ran, but the string burned her fingers and slipped. The kite dropped behind a roof and did not come back up. They stared at the red sun, now trapped beside a water tank on Mrs. Widya's house.

"We cannot climb that," Ari said. "The tiles break, and she will be angry."

Lina agreed. They knocked on Mrs. Widya's door and told the truth at once. The old woman listened, looked at their dusty knees, and sighed. "You are honest, so I will help. My son is coming this evening with a ladder. You may wait."

They waited on the front step and did small jobs so the time would feel useful. Ari swept the porch. Lina watered three pots of flowers. Mrs. Widya brought them cool water and told them about a kite she had lost in a river when she was twelve. "I cried so much that my brother was embarrassed," she said. "The river kept the kite. At least yours is only on a roof."

When her son arrived, he climbed carefully and freed the paper without tearing it. One stick was bent. The red sun was still bright. Lina thanked them more than once. At home she laid the kite on the table and straightened the stick as well as she could. The kite would fly again another day. The better ending was that she had not tried to grab it alone. Asking for help had brought the red sun back down to her hands.

questions.question: Why did the kite fail on the first try?
options: There was no wind at all.

questions.question: Where did the kite get stuck?
options: Beside a water tank on Mrs. Widya's roof

questions.question: How did they get the kite down?
options: Mrs. Widya's son used a ladder.
The wind blew it back to the field.
Ari pulled it with a broom.

list.title: The Lost Key at the Night Market
list.summary: Hana and her brother search the market for a missing key.
list.passage:
The night market opened when the heat of the day finally loosened. Lights hung in rows above the stalls, and music from a speaker mixed with the sound of chopping and laughter. Hana was there with her older brother, Fajar, to buy grilled corn and to look at the handmade bracelets. She kept her hand on the small pocket where her house key hung from a blue string.

They ate first. The corn was hot, salty, and a little sweet. Fajar paid, and Hana held both cobs while he found napkins. After they finished, she wanted to see the bracelet stall before it closed. She was halfway there when her fingers touched an empty pocket. The key and the blue string were gone.

Hana stopped so suddenly that Fajar bumped into her. "My key," she said. "It was in my pocket."

They did not search in a useful way at first. Hana wanted to run in every direction. Fajar took a breath and put his hands on her shoulders. "We go back along the same path. We ask people. We look down, not only ahead."

They returned to the corn stall. The seller shook his head, then checked the ground near his feet and the box where he kept extra napkins. Nothing. A girl selling drinks let them look under her table. A man with a guitar moved his case so they could see the pavement. Everyone was busy, but most people still helped for a moment.

Hana was close to tears when she remembered the napkins. Fajar had taken them from a metal holder near a pole. She ran there and knelt. The blue string was caught on a cracked piece of the stand, just above the ground. The key turned slowly in the air, as if it had been waiting. She closed her hand around it and laughed once, a short shaky laugh.

"Check your pocket now," Fajar said, and he was smiling too.

Hana tied the string around her wrist instead of trusting the pocket again. They still visited the bracelet stall, but she did not buy anything. She had already spent her courage for the evening. On the ride home she told Fajar the part she wanted to remember. Losing the key had been frightening. Finding it had been a plan, not magic. They had gone back, asked, and looked carefully. Next time, she would keep the knot where she could see it.

What did Fajar tell Hana to do?
options: Buy a new key at once
Go home and leave the market
Go back the same way, ask people, and look down

list.title: The Borrowed Bicycle
list.summary: Farid borrows a bicycle to collect his grandmother's medicine.
list.passage:
Farid needed to get across town before the clinic closed, because his grandmother's medicine was waiting and the last bus had already gone. His own bicycle had a bent wheel. He stood in the lane with the wheel turning in a sad oval and tried to think of another plan.

His neighbor, Mr. Salim, rolled a bicycle out of a narrow gate. It was old, painted blue, with a bell that worked and a basket that did not. "Take this," Mr. Salim said. "Bring it back before dark. The front brake is strong. The back brake is a suggestion."

Farid thanked him and tested the brakes at the corner. The front brake grabbed so hard he nearly went over the handlebars. He would remember that. He rode toward the main road, then through a market street where he had to walk the bicycle between stalls. A woman selling oranges told him he was blocking her customers. He apologized and moved faster.

At the clinic, the line was short because it was late. The nurse found the medicine, explained the dose, and made him repeat it. Once in the morning. Once after dinner. With food. Farid said it back. She nodded and taped the paper to the bag so it would not get lost in his pocket.

The ride home should have been easier. It was not. A light rain began, and the blue bicycle's back brake did exactly what Mr. Salim had promised, which was almost nothing. Farid used the front brake early and gently. He also used his shoe once, and felt foolish, and did not fall. By the time he reached the lane, his shirt was damp and the medicine was dry inside his jacket.

Mr. Salim was waiting without pretending he had not been waiting. Farid returned the bicycle, the bell still working, the basket still useless. He explained the brake and the rain. Mr. Salim waved it away. "You brought it back. You brought the medicine back. That is the borrow completed."

Farid's grandmother took her dose with a piece of bread and asked who had been kind. Farid told her the whole route, including the oranges and the shoe. She laughed until she coughed, then told him to drink water. Later he wiped the rain off the blue seat even though the bicycle was already home. It seemed like part of the thank you.

options: His wheel was bent and the last bus had gone.
Mr. Salim asked him to test the brakes.
He wanted oranges from the market.
The clinic had called his sister.

options: The front wheel was an oval.

options: Once in the morning and once after dinner, with food

list.title: The Name in the Margin
list.summary: Ina finds a pencil note in a library book and answers it on her own paper.
list.passage:
Ina liked library books that other people had already loved. A turned-down corner or a faded underline made the book feel less like a new task and more like a conversation. She knew she was not supposed to write in library books. She never did. She only read what was already there.

On Wednesday she borrowed a novel about a girl who moved to a city by the sea. On page forty, in the margin, someone had written a name in pencil: "For Lila, who hated endings." The handwriting was small and careful. Ina stared at it. It was not a note about the story. It was a note to a person.

She asked the librarian, Mr. Andra, whether he knew a Lila. He thought for a moment. "There was a student volunteer with that name two years ago. She shelved books on weekends. I do not have her address. I should not give it to you even if I did."

"I do not need her address," Ina said. "I just wanted to know she was real."

Mr. Andra smiled. "Most names in margins are real. That is why they surprise us."

Ina read the novel slowly. The girl in the story did hate the last chapter. The city flooded, and the ending refused to be tidy. In the final margin there was no more writing, only a tiny star. Ina added nothing. She closed the book and held it for a minute.

The next week she came back with a plan that did not break the rules. She wrote a short letter on her own paper. It said she had found the note, that she also distrusted tidy endings, and that the book was safe. She did not sign her full address. She signed her first name and the words "a reader." Mr. Andra agreed to keep the letter in the volunteer drawer, in case Lila ever returned.

"And if she does not?" Ina asked.

"Then the letter waits," he said. "Books do that well. Paper can learn the habit."

Months passed. Ina borrowed other novels. She stopped checking the drawer every time, then checked once more in June. The letter was gone. In its place was a postcard of the sea with one sentence on the back: "I did hate the ending. Thank you for not writing in the book." There was no name. Ina did not need one. The margin had started the conversation, and the postcard had finished it without spoiling the page.

questions.question: What was written in the margin on page forty?
options: Do not write in this book.

questions.question: Why did Ina write on her own paper?
options: The pencil in the book had faded.
She was not supposed to write in a library book.
Mr. Andra asked her to copy the novel.
Lila had left her a blank postcard.

questions.question: What did Ina find in the drawer in June?
options: A postcard thanking her for not writing in the book
The novel with a new ending

list.title: The Last Seat
list.summary: Karim shares a train seat with a woman whose son missed the train.
list.passage:
The evening train was crowded. People stood in the aisle with bags between their feet. Karim held a box of books for his cousin and tried not to hit anyone when the train swayed. He looked down the carriage and saw one empty seat beside an elderly woman. A paper bag sat on it.

He moved closer. "Is this seat free?"

The woman looked at the bag, then at him, then at the box in his arms. "It was for my son. He missed the train. Sit, before someone less polite decides for us."

Karim sat. The box went on his lap. The woman, who told him her name was Bu Rini, kept one hand on the paper bag as if it still marked a place. She asked what was in the box. He said they were secondhand novels for a small reading room his cousin was starting in a rented garage.

"A garage," she said. "That is how serious things begin. My son repairs radios in a garage. He was supposed to bring me a part. The part can wait. His excuse will be creative."

They talked as the stations passed. Bu Rini had strong opinions about stories that ended too sweetly. Karim disagreed about one famous book and then realized she had read it more carefully than he had. He admitted it. She looked pleased, not victorious. "Good," she said. "A reader who can change his mind is still a reader."

At her stop she stood and nearly forgot the paper bag. Karim handed it to her. Inside, he glimpsed an orange and a folded cloth. She took the bag and studied him for a second. "If the garage ever has a chair that does not wobble, I will visit. I will bring a book you are wrong about."

"Please do," Karim said.

The seat did not stay empty. A tired man took it at once. Karim held the box and watched Bu Rini on the platform, smaller and then gone. He thought about the son who had missed the train, and about rooms that start as garages. When he got off, his arms ached and his head was full. The last seat had been a small kindness with a paper bag on it. He hoped the reading room would have room for that kind of luck.

questions.question: Why was the seat empty?
options: Bu Rini's son had missed the train.
Karim had reserved it for the books.
A tired man had just left it.

questions.question: What was inside Karim's box?
What did Bu Rini respect about Karim?
options: He could change his mind about a book.
He stood in the aisle the whole way.

list.title: Soup on a Rainy Day
list.summary: Mira and her father cook vegetable soup and learn to wait.
list.passage:
It rained all morning, so Mira and her father stayed in the kitchen. They decided to make vegetable soup. Mira washed the carrots and the potatoes. Her father cut the onions. The onions made Mira's eyes sting, and she laughed and stepped back.

"Cut slowly," her father said. "A sharp knife is safer when you pay attention."

Mira watched the pot. They added water, salt, and the vegetables. Then her father turned the heat down. "Let it simmer," he said. "If it boils too hard, the potatoes break too soon." Mira did not know the word simmer. He showed her the small bubbles that rose gently and did not jump.

While they waited, Mira set the table. She put out two bowls, two spoons, and a ladle on a plate. The ladle was big. She liked the way it could hold a whole spoonful of soup and more. She also cut a little bread. The crust was hard, so she pressed the knife down with care.

After twenty minutes her father tasted the soup with a clean spoon. He shook his head. "It needs salt, but only a pinch. We can add more later. We cannot take it out." Mira added a pinch and stirred. The second taste was better. The carrots were soft. The potatoes were still in pieces.

They ate by the window. Rain ran down the glass. The soup was hot, so Mira blew on each spoonful. Her father said that cooking was mostly waiting and tasting. Mira thought about that. She had wanted the soup to be ready at once. The slow pot had done a better job than a rush would have done.

When they finished, Mira washed the ladle and the bowls. She left the pot to cool. The rain was still falling, but the kitchen smelled like carrots and pepper, and the afternoon no longer felt cold.
